title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
claim: A staged training recipe quantizes inputs into discrete codes, then trains a controller and policy that compose at test time.
layout: 2 boxed panels (Training above, Evaluation below), left-to-right block flow, stage labels
description: A block diagram split into two gray-bordered boxes. The top 'Training' box has three stages. Stage I, on the left, takes an action chunk a_{t:t+L} through a blue 1-D Conv and an FSQ quantizer, which together are labeled Encoder φ. The resulting code k and state s_t go into a blue trapezoid Decoder ψ that outputs x_{t+L}. On the right, Stage II is a green Low-Level Control π_A box. It takes k and s_t and outputs a_t. Stage III is an orange High-Level Policy π_Z box. It takes s_t and goal g and outputs k. The bottom 'Evaluation' box chains the orange high-level policy into the green low-level controller: (s_t, g) → k → (k, s_t) → a_t. Color coding is consistent across stages, with blue for quantizer, green for controller and orange for policy. The eye goes first to the bold stage headings and the large blue Stage I blocks.
caption: Three-stage training and evaluation overview of our proposed framework. Stage I: Action chunk quantization, optimized for predicting next-state features. Stage II: Learning to execute the skill codes. Stage III: Training a goal-conditioned discrete policy that produces skill codes. During evaluation, the high-level policy πZ produces discrete skill codes that are converted to continuous actions by the trained low-level controller and are executed in the environment.
abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.
